facts.text: Earth's magnetic field last reversed, ending the Matuyama chron (C1r) and opening the present Brunhes chron (C1n).
Estimates of the flip's length range from within a human lifetime to several thousand years, or about 22,000 years.
Its apparent duration at any one site can vary tenfold with geomagnetic latitude and local quirks of the field.
The reversal marks the GSSP for the base of the Chibanian Stage at the Chiba section in Japan, ratified in 2020.
It is a standard tie-point for dating ocean sediment cores and volcanic rocks.

title: Mammal turnover at the Early–Middle Pleistocene transition

facts.text: With Sinomastodon's extinction in East Asia, gomphotheres vanished from Afro-Eurasia, though they survived in the Americas into the Late Pleistocene.
A major extinction of European carnivorous mammals, including the giant hyena Pachycrocuta, occurred around the same transition.
True horses migrated out of North America into Eurasia at the Early–Middle Pleistocene boundary.
In Europe the mammoth Mammuthus meridionalis died out and was replaced by the Asian steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii.
The elephant genus Palaeoloxodon spread from Africa into Eurasia, including the first straight-tusked elephants (Palaeoloxodon antiquus).

facts.text: The temporal range of the clawed perissodactyls Ancylopoda (chalicotheres) runs from the Eocene into the Middle Pleistocene.

title: Bishop Tuff eruption forms Long Valley Caldera

facts.text: A VEI-7 eruption in eastern California released about 600 km³ of material, which cooled into the Bishop Tuff.
Draining the magma chamber caused collapse, leaving Long Valley Caldera, about 32 by 18 km and one of Earth's largest calderas.
Pyroclastic flows burned and buried thousands of square miles, and ash blanketed much of the western United States.

title: Lava dams block the Colorado in the Grand Canyon
article: Geology of the Grand Canyon area

facts.text: Over 150 basaltic lava flows dammed the Colorado River at least 13 times between 725,000 and 100,000 years ago.
The dams formed in weeks and stood up to 610 m high and 138 km long.
How long they held back lakes is debated.

facts.text: The Mid-Pleistocene Transition, under way since about 1.25 million years ago, was complete by about 0.7 million years ago.
Ice-age rhythm shifted from 41,000-year cycles to asymmetric, high-amplitude cycles averaging 100,000 years, making climate swings more extreme.
Interglacials after the transition had more atmospheric carbon dioxide than those before it.
Since about 600,000 years ago, six major glacial periods have lowered sea level by up to 120 m, exposing continental margins.

title: Acheulean hand axes appear in Europe

facts.text: Typical Acheulean bifaces (hand axes) appeared in Europe about 700,000 years ago.
Their sudden arrival has been argued to reflect influence from Africa rather than purely local invention.
Late Acheulean culture, usually tied to the dispersal of Homo heidelbergensis, spread across Europe and Africa by the beginning of the Middle Pleistocene.

title: Ancestors of the Flores 'hobbit' at Mata Menge

facts.text: Teeth and a partial jaw from hominins thought ancestral to Homo floresiensis lived at Mata Menge on Flores about 700,000 years ago.
They were as small as or smaller than the later Liang Bua remains, so the species' small size stayed stable for hundreds of thousands of years.

verification.title: Early evolution of small body size in Homo floresiensis

title: Archaic 'ghost' lineage splits from modern humans
article: Interbreeding between archaic and modern humans

facts.text: An archaic hominin population broke away from the modern human lineage around 700,000 years ago.
Its DNA later entered some sub-Saharan hunter-gatherer groups, such as the Biaka and San, about 35,000 years ago.

facts.text: During the first glacial stage of the Cromerian Complex, sedimentation by the Baltic River System in the Netherlands ended, marking the end of the Eridanos.
Repeated Scandinavian ice caps destroyed its source area and gouged the basin where the Baltic Sea later formed.
At its height about 2 Ma, the Eridanos ran some 2,700 km from Lapland across the Baltic region to a vast delta in western Europe.

facts.text: Marine Isotope Stage 16 was one of the two most extreme Quaternary glaciations by global ice volume, on par with MIS 12.
Ocean temperatures, though, were only about as cold as in the neighbouring glacials MIS 14 and MIS 18.
On the East European Plain the Don ice sheet reached the middle and lower Don basin at about 50° N, its greatest extent there.

facts.text: Genetic distances suggest Denisovans and Neanderthals diverged from each other about 640,000 years ago.
Their nuclear DNA shows they were closer to each other than either was to modern humans.
Homo heidelbergensis is usually considered the direct ancestor of both.

facts.text: Yellowstone's third-cycle climactic eruption produced the Lava Creek Tuff and created the present Yellowstone Caldera.
Rated VEI 8, it ejected more than 1,000 km³ of rock, dust and volcanic ash.
Its ash bed spread over 3–4 million km², and debris up to two metres deep covered a large part of North America.
It capped several hundred thousand years of rhyolitic volcanism and struck near the shift from glacial MIS 16 to interglacial MIS 15.
Eruptions of this size happen somewhere on Earth about every 50,000 to 100,000 years.

article: Geology of the Lassen volcanic area

facts.text: More than 130 km³ of rhyolite magma erupted violently from the Lassen area of California, with huge pyroclastic flows and an ash plume tens of kilometres high.
Recent studies put the Rockland ash at up to 326.7 km³, over twice the Mazama ash.

title: First complete Great Barrier Reef structures

facts.text: The earliest evidence of complete reef structures on the Great Barrier Reef dates to about 600,000 years ago.
Coral skeleton deposits there date back about half a million years.

title: Homo heidelbergensis evolves

facts.text: Homo heidelbergensis evolved about 600,000 years ago in Africa as a derived form of Homo erectus.
Fossils from the MIS 15 interglacial (621–563 ka) include Heidelberg Man and the Bodo cranium.
It was the likely ancestor of Denisovans and Neanderthals, and perhaps of modern humans.
Some scholars place the first symbolic communication with this species.
It is a controversial, poorly defined species; the tangle of Middle Pleistocene Homo forms is nicknamed the 'muddle in the middle'.

contested_note: Its own article calls H. heidelbergensis a controversial, poorly defined species whose classification is disputed.

title: Modern Cascade stratovolcanoes begin to grow

facts.text: About half a million years ago an older generation of Cascade volcanoes died and many of today's stratovolcanoes began growing.
Glacier Peak and Mount Shasta started about 600,000 years ago, Rainier and Hood 500,000, Adams 450,000 and Mazama 420,000.
Newberry Volcano and Mount Tehama also began forming about 600,000 years ago.

sources.title: Geology of the Lassen volcanic area

facts.text: The woolly mammoth evolved from the steppe mammoth, Mammuthus trogontherii, in Siberia by around 600,000–500,000 years ago.
Its lineage had begun to diverge about 800,000 years ago; molars with 26 ridges, the woolly mammoth's mark, appeared about 400,000 years ago.
Siberian mammoths over a million years old already carried many of the woolly mammoth's genes for tolerating cold.
Columbian mammoths descend half from woolly mammoths and half from the Krestovka lineage, which hybridised more than 420,000 years ago.
Woolly mammoth numbers crashed around 280,000 years ago, then recovered.

title: Lonar crater impact, India

facts.text: A hypervelocity meteorite impact blasted a crater 1.8 km wide and 150 m deep into Deccan basalt in Maharashtra.
Argon–argon dating gives 570 ± 47 ka, far older than an earlier estimate of 52 ± 6 ka.
It holds India's only crater lake of meteoritic origin.

contested_note: The argon–argon age is disputed, because inherited argon may have made the crater look older than it is.

verification.title: 40Ar/39Ar age of the Lonar crater and consequence for the geochronology of planetary impacts

facts.text: Archaic humans lived in the Caune de l'Arago, a limestone cave at Tautavel in France, from about 550,000 to 400,000 years ago.
Almost all the human remains come from bed G, dated by uranium–thorium to 455,000 years ago.
The landscape swung repeatedly between temperate forest and cold, dry grassy steppe.

title: Engraved shell at Trinil, possibly the first art

facts.text: A Pseudodon shell from Trinil, Java, engraved with geometric markings 546,000–436,000 years ago, could be the earliest known art-making.
The Trinil Homo erectus population also made scrapers from Pseudodon shells, possibly opening them with shark teeth.
Homo erectus lived at Trinil 540,000–430,000 years ago, part of a long occupation of Java that began at Sangiran 1.51–0.93 million years ago.

facts.text: MIS 13 was an interglacial covering the late Cromerian in Britain, about 524,000–474,000 years ago.
It began with birch, pine and spruce, and followed the relatively warm glacial MIS 14 before the cold MIS 12 glacial.
Boxgrove then lay on the coast, below chalk cliffs, amid mudflats that gave way to woodland and grassland.
The first brown bears appeared around 0.5 million years ago.
Around 500,000 years ago, early humans often called Homo heidelbergensis came to Europe from Africa and eventually evolved into Neanderthals.
Boxgrove in Sussex, about 500,000 years old, is the earliest site in Britain with fossils of Homo.
These humans pushed north beyond the 50th parallel, to Boxgrove and Eartham Pit.
Populations had dispersed into Europe by 700,000 years ago, spreading Late Acheulean tools, and more permanent groups settled north of 45°N about then.
Settlements became more permanent by 500,000 years ago, and occupation grew much more frequent afterwards.

conflicts.note: Boxgrove deposition at the end of MIS 13

title: Lake Victoria and the White Nile take shape

facts.text: Around 0.5 million years ago Lake Victoria assumed roughly its modern shape.
The lakes plateau tilted north and began draining intermittently toward Egypt, roughly along the modern White Nile.
Paleolakes formed where the Sudd swamps now lie.
The Elster glaciation, the Anglian in Britain, was the oldest ice age to glaciate North Germany and much of Europe on a large scale.
MIS 12 was globally the stronger glacial of its era, ranking with MIS 16 among the two largest Quaternary ice volumes.
An ice sheet filled much of the North Sea, with a large proglacial lake to its south fed by the Rhine, Scheldt and Thames.
Great Britain was widely glaciated, and the glaciation ended the long, relatively warm Cromerian Complex.

conflicts.note: Geiseltal page; Elster dated to a different window

facts.text: The steppe-tundra biome first emerged during the MIS 12 glacial, uniting animals of the northern tundra and Central Asian steppe.
It would repeatedly expand and contract with later glacial cycles.

title: First Channel megaflood breaches the Dover Strait

facts.text: An ice dam to the north backed river water into a vast lake in the southern North Sea, held by a chalk ridge from the Weald to Artois.
During the Anglian glaciation the lake broke through, the first of two megafloods that cut through the Weald–Artois Anticline.
The flood diverted the Rhine into the English Channel; sonar shows deeply gouged channels and streamlined islands on the seabed.
It ended the land bridge between Britain and France, though links returned at low sea level.

title: Early Neanderthals at Sima de los Huesos

facts.text: Hominins at Sima de los Huesos in Atapuerca, Spain, dated to about 430,000 years ago, were early members of the Neanderthal line.
They yield the oldest known human DNA.
Their anatomy suggests many Neanderthal traits evolved by the mid-Middle Pleistocene.
They probably lived through one of the coldest glacial phases of the last million years, which dried out Iberia.

verification.title: Neandertal roots: Cranial and chronological evidence from Sima de los Huesos

facts.text: MIS 11 was the longest and warmest interglacial of the last 500,000 years, possibly twice as long as others.
It saw the highest-amplitude deglacial warming of the last 5 million years.
South Greenland nearly fully deglaciated, adding 4.5–6 m of sea-level equivalent around 410,000–400,000 years ago.
High-latitude seas were warm, thermohaline circulation strong, sea level higher than now, and coral reefs expanded.
It matches the Hoxnian in Britain, Holsteinian in Central Europe and Yarmouthian in North America; Swanscombe Man dates from it.

conflicts.note: Holstein was historically also correlated with MIS 9

facts.text: From about 0.4 Ma, Homo heidelbergensis developed its own tool industry, the Clactonian.

sources.title: Early expansions of hominins out of Africa

facts.text: The earliest specimens of the modern grey wolf date to around 400,000 years ago, possibly as early as 1 million years ago.
Between 400,000 and 300,000 years ago dholes and wolves were similar in size, but wolves were slowly growing larger.

title: Hominins master the habitual use of fire
article: Control of fire by early humans

facts.text: Reliable evidence of regular fire use appears in the archaeological record about 400,000 years ago; before that, fire use was sparse.
The shift may mark true domestication of fire and fire-starting technology, or simply better ways of keeping fires alight.
The oldest definitive fire-making, about 400,000 years ago at a Neanderthal site in eastern England, left burnt soil, fire-cracked handaxes and pyrite for striking sparks.
European caves show no regular fire before 400,000–300,000 years ago; good evidence follows the MIS 9 interglacial, about 340,000 years ago.
Fire became widespread in the Middle Paleolithic, and humans were cooking food by about 250,000 years ago.

sources.title: Control of fire by early humans

facts.text: The Saale complex, the middle of northern Europe's three great Scandinavian ice-sheet glaciations, spanned about 400,000 to 130,000 years ago.
It spans several glacial cycles separated by warmer periods, opening with the Fuhne cold phase and the Dömnitz interglacial.
Its latter part coincides with the global Penultimate Glacial Period.
Britain's equivalent, the Wolstonian, lasted about 374,000–130,000 years ago; the Alpine Riss is paralleled by MIS 10, 8 and 6.

verification.title: Timing of the Saalian- and Elsterian glacial cycles and the implications for Middle – Pleistocene hominin presence in central Europe

facts.text: Neanderthals evolved by about 350,000 years ago.
Middle Pleistocene European fossils, such as those from Sima de los Huesos, are seen as ancestral to them.
Their characteristic teeth had evolved by about 300,000 years ago.
They lived across Europe and the Near East from about 300,000 years ago.
Some Neanderthal traits appeared only near the start of the Late Pleistocene, possibly with the species' full speciation.
A VEI-8 eruption sequence, lasting under a thousand years, produced 1,200–2,000 km³ of tephra on New Zealand's North Island.
It created the Whakamaru Caldera, about 30 by 40 km, just north of today's Lake Taupō.
It opened a burst of under 100,000 years in which the Taupō Volcanic Zone erupted over 4,000 km³ in total.
This was part of an ignimbrite flare-up from about 350,000 to 240,000 years ago.

facts.text: MIS 9 was an interglacial, the Purfleet Interglacial in Britain, and the last period of the Lower Paleolithic.
East Antarctica's Wilkes Basin lost enough ice to raise sea level by about 0.9 m.
Carbon dioxide was probably higher than in MIS 11.

verification.title: A Pliocene‐Pleistocene stack of 57 globally distributed benthic δ 18 O records
verification.note: The LR04 abstract's dates are about the stack's length and its precession phase, not the MIS 9 boundaries.

title: Schöningen spears, the oldest complete wooden weapons

facts.text: Ten wooden weapons of spruce and pine from a lignite mine at Schöningen, Germany, are the oldest complete wooden weapons known, found with butchered horse bones.
Probably used for both throwing and thrusting, they were made by Homo heidelbergensis or early Neanderthals and point to sophisticated hunting and forward planning.
Their age is disputed: first put at 400,000–380,000 years, then 337,000–300,000 by thermoluminescence, and about 200,000 years by a 2025 study.

contested_note: The spears' age is disputed, with estimates from about 400,000 to 200,000 years.

title: Homo naledi in the Rising Star Cave

facts.text: Homo naledi, a small-brained archaic human, lived in South Africa's Rising Star Cave system 335,000–236,000 years ago, in the Middle Pleistocene.
Because its brain was so small, the fossils were first assumed to be 1–2 million years old; its line branched from other Homo by 900,000 years ago.
The Dinaledi Chamber holds over 1,500 bones from at least 15 individuals, the largest find of a single hominin species in Africa.
Some researchers suggest it deliberately placed its dead in the remote chamber, a claim still debated.

facts.text: By about 320,000 years ago people at Olorgesailie moved obsidian long distances, used pigments and possibly made projectile points.
This roughly matches the earliest Homo sapiens fossils, suggesting complex behaviour began with the species.
After a long stable spell, the local environment grew more variable around 400,000 years ago as tectonics broke up the landscape.
By around 200,000 years ago, Middle Paleolithic toolmakers had developed the Levallois, or prepared-core, technique, more elaborate than Acheulean methods.
Levallois-type tools occur in Levantine cave layers dated 250,000–140,000 years ago.
In Europe the Mousterian, built on the Levallois technique, appeared around 320,000 years ago and displaced the Acheulean there by about 125,000 years ago.

facts.text: Fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, once thought Neanderthal, are now assigned to Homo sapiens, with a weighted average age of 315,000 years.
Burnt flint tools found with them were dated by thermoluminescence to about 315,000 years ago.
They are by far the oldest known H. sapiens, showing modern humans lived across Africa 100,000 years earlier than once thought.
Homo sapiens arose in Africa from a lineage close to early Homo heidelbergensis.
Early H. sapiens may have spread across Africa, with several regions contributing; the Florisbad skull, about 259,000 years old, is also early H. sapiens.

title: Middle Stone Age and Middle Paleolithic begin

facts.text: Africa's Middle Stone Age began around 300,000 years ago and is linked to anatomically modern or nearly modern Homo sapiens.
Its European counterpart, the Middle Paleolithic, broadly spans 300,000 to 50,000 years ago.
The Chibanian thus spans the Lower-to-Middle Paleolithic transition.
At Pinnacle Point, South Africa, Middle Stone Age Homo sapiens cooked shellfish and heat-treated silcrete in fire to improve their tools by about 164,000 years ago.
Evidence of hafting, in both Europe and Africa, becomes much more common after 300,000 years ago.

facts.text: Gigantopithecus, a giant Asian relative of the orangutan, died out about 300,000 years ago.
The great ape lived in central and southern China from about 2 million years ago; its youngest remains, from Shuangtan and Gongjishan Caves, are 295,000–215,000 years old.
After about 400,000 years ago it survived only in Guangxi; retreating subtropical forest, and perhaps archaic humans, likely drove it extinct.

facts.text: Early Middle Paleolithic tools, including cores and scrapers, were left in Denisova Cave, Siberia, about 287,000 years ago.
Denisovan DNA from the cave's sediments dates back to 217,000 years ago.
Child hand- and footprints at Quesang, Tibet, dated 226,000–169,000 years ago, may be Denisovan and are the plateau's oldest human traces.
A 200,000-year-old Denisovan molar carries about 5% of its genome from a previously unknown Neanderthal population.
Denisovans ranged across Asia from about 200,000 to 32,000 years ago.

title: Possible first out-of-Africa wave of Homo sapiens
article: Recent African origin of modern humans

facts.text: Early Homo sapiens, or a close relative, may have first left Africa as early as 270,000 years ago, the first of several waves.
The idea rests on Neanderthal mitochondrial genomes being closer to H. sapiens than to Denisovans.
Neanderthal genes in modern humans descend from at least two interbreeding episodes outside Africa, the first about 250,000 years ago.

sources.title: Recent African origin of modern humans

verification.title: Deeply divergent archaic mitochondrial genome provides lower time boundary for African gene flow into Neanderthals

facts.text: MIS 7 had three phases of very low ice volume and high temperatures; MIS 7e peaked about 237,000–228,000 years ago.
It was the coldest interglacial since the Mid-Brunhes Event, with MIS 7e about 1.4 °C below pre-industrial global temperature.
Its start, Termination III about 243,000 years ago, included a Younger Dryas-like cold reversal.
A VEI-7 eruption ejected more than 340 km³ of rhyolitic Mamaku ignimbrite, and the Rotorua Caldera collapsed as the magma chamber emptied.
Within days or weeks a second eruption from the same magma body burst out at Ohakuri, about 30 km south.
The sequence formed the basin of Lake Rotorua.

verification.title: Double trouble: Paired ignimbrite eruptions and collateral subsidence in the Taupo Volcanic Zone, New Zealand

title: The Mammoth Site sinkhole trap, South Dakota

facts.text: A cavern in limestone near Hot Springs, South Dakota, collapsed into a steep sinkhole at least 20 m deep, filled by a warm artesian pond.
Luminescence dating in 2026 put its formation at about 232,000–160,000 years ago, in MIS 7 and 6.
Its sediments trapped and buried Pleistocene animals, including 58 Columbian and 3 woolly mammoths.

facts.text: Mesotherium, the last mesotheriid and last of the Typotheria, has its final records around 220,000 years ago.
Afterwards Toxodontidae was the only notoungulate family to survive into the Late Pleistocene.

title: Earliest modern human maternal lineage (Mitochondrial Eve)

facts.text: Mitochondrial DNA studies trace the earliest maternal lineage of Homo sapiens to about 200,000 years ago.
They point to the Makgadikgadi lake region of southern Africa as the homeland, followed by expansion about 70,000 years later.
Another estimate puts Mitochondrial Eve at 99,000–148,000 years ago and the Y-chromosome ancestor at 120,000–156,000, both in Africa.

sources.title: Recent African origin of modern humans

contested_note: The claim that the Makgadikgadi region was the homeland of modern humans remains a matter of controversy.

facts.text: The woolly mammoth emerged in the mid-to-late Middle Pleistocene and replaced its forerunner, the steppe mammoth Mammuthus trogontherii.
In Europe, woolly mammoths had fully replaced steppe mammoths by around 200,000 years ago.
In North America, woolly mammoths were among the northern specialists that spread south of Alaska with bison during the Rancholabrean.
Neanderthals lived alongside mammoths and used their bones for tools and building, as at La Cotte de St Brelade about 200,000 years ago.

verification.title: Mammoth evolution in the late Middle Pleistocene: The Mammuthus trogontherii-primigenius transition in Europe

title: Early modern humans at Omo and Herto, Ethiopia

facts.text: The Omo Kibish remains from Ethiopia, about 195,000 years old, were long held to be the oldest Homo sapiens fossils.
They supported an East African origin of modern humans around 200,000 years ago.
Herto Man, also from Ethiopia and about 160,000 years old, is further early physical evidence of the Middle Stone Age.
Steppe bison, ancestors of the American bison, crossed the Bering land bridge into North America around 195,000–135,000 years ago.
Their arrival marks the start of the Rancholabrean faunal stage, defined by the presence of Bison.
Bison first appeared in northwestern North America during the Illinoian, then spread across the continent in the Sangamonian.
They expanded south of Alaska alongside caribou, muskoxen, moose and woolly mammoths.

facts.text: The Penultimate Glacial Period ran from about 194,000 years ago, at the end of the MIS 7 interglacial, to about 135,000 years ago.
Its maximum, around 140,000 years ago, was Eurasia's most extensive glaciation in 400,000 years; a thick ice sheet over northern Europe slashed vegetation.
High latitudes were colder, and the tropics warmer, than at the Last Glacial Maximum.
It is the coldest, last part of the Saale/Wolstonian complex; in North America the Illinoian Stage, OSL-dated to MIS 6, matches it.
The Bull Lake glaciation of the Rocky Mountains, about 200,000–130,000 years ago, was concurrent.

title: Early Homo sapiens in the Levant (Misliya Cave)

facts.text: A jawbone with eight teeth from Misliya Cave on Mount Carmel, possibly Homo sapiens, was dated in 2018 to 177,000 years ago.
It may mean modern humans moved in and out of the Levant several times, possibly even before 200,000 years ago.
A 210,000-year-old skull fragment from Apidima Cave, Greece, has been read as H. sapiens, though the idea has limited recognition.

title: Second Channel megaflood makes Britain an island

facts.text: A second megaflood broke through the Weald–Artois chalk ridge during the Saalian/Wolstonian glaciation (MIS 6).
Cohen and Hijma date the ridge's final destruction to the Saalian peak around 160,000 years ago, ending with a second meltwater lake about 130,000 years ago.
A lake held back in the Doggerland region burst through, cutting the Strait of Dover.
Afterwards Britain became an island whenever sea level was high.

facts.text: From 135,000 years ago, megadroughts struck tropical Africa, pushing humans toward the coasts and onto other continents.
By the MIS 5 megadrought, 130,000 years ago, Africa held two ancestral human population clusters, including mtDNA haplogroup L0 in the south.

title: Termination II meltwater ends the Penultimate Glacial

facts.text: Meltwater pulse 2B, about 133,000 years ago, substantially weakened the Indian Summer Monsoon.
During an insolation maximum 133,000–130,000 years ago, meltwater from the Dnieper and Volga joined the Black and Caspian Seas.
This deglaciation, Termination II, included a cold reversal similar to the Younger Dryas.

facts.text: About 130,000 years ago the Aso-3 eruption in Japan produced about 96 km³ of magma (dense-rock equivalent).
It was one of four great pyroclastic-flow eruptions, between 270,000 and 90,000 years ago, that formed the Aso caldera.
The earlier Aso-1 (about 266,000 years ago) and Aso-2 (about 141,000) each erupted about 32 km³.
Burials at Krapina, Croatia, date to about 130,000 years ago.
Some anthropologists see in such burials a developing belief in an afterlife and a concern for the dead.
